blocks.text: Dear Lisa:

Thank you for the time you gave us over the past several weeks. We learned a good deal about the company's pension plan in those conversations, and we are glad that {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} has asked us to do this work. You told us that contributions to the plan have been decided one year at a time, with no written rule behind them, and that the company's budget has had to absorb the result. A funding policy gives those decisions a footing. Below we have put in writing what we understand the study to be and the terms on which we will do it.
The question we have been asked

The question is how much the company should put into the plan each year, and by what rule. The law sets a minimum contribution. It also limits the deduction for contributions above a certain level. Between those bounds the choice belongs to the company, and our part is to help it make that choice on purpose and write it down.
We see the study in four parts.

1. We will review the plan's recent funding history: what was contributed, when it was deposited, and how each contribution compared with the minimum the law required and the most it allowed as a deduction.

2. We will work with you to state the company's objectives for the policy in writing. A steadier budget, the cost of PBGC premiums, and the plan's funded level are the ones you have raised so far. We will not model any alternative until you have confirmed the list.

3. We will project contributions, funded status, and PBGC premiums over a span of future years, under the current practice and under alternative policies. Each policy will be tested under more than one set of economic conditions.
4. We will recommend a policy in a written report, set out the risks that come with it and with each alternative, and meet with you to go through the report.

Some related work is outside this letter. We have not been asked to value the plan for the current year, to prepare figures for the company's financial statements, to advise on how the plan's assets are invested, or to propose changes to the benefits. If you want any of these, we will propose it separately.
What we will work from

A projection starts from where the plan stands today. We will build ours from the most recent actuarial valuation and the information behind it. So that your staff can begin gathering files, these are the items we will need first:
1. The most recent valuation report and the participant data used to prepare it.
2. The plan document and each amendment adopted since that valuation.
3. Trust statements showing assets, contributions, benefit payments, and expenses for the most recent plan years.
4. A record of each contribution the company has made in recent years, with the amount and the date it was deposited.
5. The plan's current investment policy statement.

We will rely on these materials without auditing them. We will check them for completeness and for consistency with one another. If we find a problem, we will tell you what it is and what we did about it, and the report will record it.
The standards we work under

We will perform the study in accordance with the Actuarial Standards of Practice that apply to it. Those that bear most directly are ASOP No. 4, on measuring pension obligations and determining contributions; No. 51, on assessing and disclosing risk; No. 56, on modeling; No. 23, on data quality; and No. 41, on actuarial communications.

A projection is not a forecast. Ours will depend on assumptions about investment returns, interest rates, and the people in the plan, and actual experience will differ from every one of them. The report will say which results come from the data, which come from assumptions, and which are our judgment.
Where our recommendation depends on a particular assumption, the report will say so in a paragraph of its own, so that the company can see what would change if that assumption proves wrong.
Who will do the work

I will lead the study, review each stage of the work, and sign the report. Michelle Banks, an Actuarial Associate, will check the data and the benefit calculations, and she will be the person your staff hear from about files. David Sherman, a Senior Analyst, will build the projection model and run each policy through it.
You will hear from Michelle and David most often. If anything about the work concerns you, I would like you to call me.
Start date and fee

We will begin on {{fact:f:E-2023-001.start}}. We expect the study to run about four months. How quickly the data arrive, and how long it takes us to agree the objectives with you, will decide most of that.
Our fee for the study this letter describes is {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}. It is a fixed fee.
Fees and payment

We will bill monthly for the work done in the month, and the total billed will not exceed the fixed fee. Invoices are payable within thirty days. Any further scenarios or meetings beyond those described here will be agreed with you in writing before we start them, and billed at our standard hourly rates.
Term and termination

The engagement begins on the start date above and ends when we have delivered the final report and met with you to discuss it. Either of us may end it sooner by written notice to the other. If that happens, the company will pay for the work done through the date of the notice, and we will send you a written account of where the work stood.
Confidentiality

The participant data will contain personal information about the company's employees, former employees, and their beneficiaries. We will keep it on systems with restricted access, use it only for this study, and not disclose it outside our firm without your written consent unless the law requires us to. The report is prepared for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} and for the plan. You may share it with the plan's auditors and advisers, but no one else may rely on it without our written consent.
Limitation of liability

We will do the work with the care and skill expected of a qualified actuary. We are not responsible for errors that arise from data or information given to us that was incomplete or inaccurate. Our total liability arising from this engagement is limited to the fees paid to us under this letter, except where the law does not allow such a limit.
Governing law
This letter is governed by the laws of the state where our principal office is located.

Please read the letter through. If it matches what we discussed, sign it below on behalf of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} and return a copy to me. If any part reads differently from your understanding, call me before you sign and we will put it right. When the signed copy comes back, Michelle Banks will send you the data request.
We are looking forward to working with you and your colleagues.
Yours truly,

To: Robert Lawrence, David Sherman
From: Michelle Banks
Re: Funding policy study for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}}, opening the work
What the study is for

The signed engagement letter is on file, and the study opened on {{fact:f:E-2023-001.start}}. {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} wants a written funding policy for its pension plan, meaning a rule for how much to contribute each year in place of the year-by-year decisions it has made until now.

Our job is to show the company what each candidate rule would mean for its contributions, the plan's funded status, and its PBGC premiums, and then to recommend one. Robert Lawrence leads and will sign the report.

The letter leaves out the annual valuation, figures for the company's financial statements, investment advice, and changes to the benefits. If the company raises any of these with you, note it and pass it to Robert Lawrence rather than taking it on within the study.
Lisa Hubbard, the company's Chief Operating Officer, is our client contact. Every request to the company goes through her, so that her staff see one list from us and not three.
The work, in the order we expect to do it

items: 1. Data intake and checks. Michelle Banks. Collect the items listed in the engagement letter, log each file as it arrives, and check the participant data against the summaries in the most recent valuation report.

2. Baseline. David Sherman. Code the plan provisions and reproduce the liabilities and the minimum required contribution shown in that report, so the projections start from a position the company already recognizes.
3. Objectives. Robert Lawrence, with Michelle Banks keeping the notes. Agree with Lisa Hubbard, in writing, what the company wants the policy to achieve.

4. Projections. David Sherman, reviewed by Robert Lawrence. Project the current practice and each alternative policy under a central set of assumptions, then under the economic scenarios we agree with the client.

5. Report and presentation. Robert Lawrence, with Michelle Banks drafting the sections on data and methods. Write the recommendation, disclose the risks of each policy, and present the results to the company.

blocks.text: Items 1 and 2 can run side by side once the valuation report arrives. Item 4 should not begin until the objectives in item 3 are confirmed, because the alternatives we test depend on them.
How we will keep the record
I will open a data log with the first file. Each entry records what arrived, what we checked, and any question we sent back, so the report's section on data reliance can be written from the log.
Anything we assume in place of missing or doubtful data goes in the log as an assumption, with the reason for it. It stays marked that way until the company confirms or corrects it.
Before the end of next week
1. I will send the data request to Lisa Hubbard, built from the list in the engagement letter, and ask that files come through our secure file transfer site.
2. David Sherman will set up the projection model from our pension template, ready for the plan provisions once the plan document is in hand.
3. Robert Lawrence will propose times to Lisa Hubbard for the conversation about objectives. It may work best as part of a working session held once the baseline is in place.
4. Each of us should read the valuation report as soon as it arrives. Please send questions about it to me, and I will pass them to the company as one list.
If any of this differs from your reading of the engagement letter, please tell me before the data request goes out.
Hi Lisa,

Thank you for the files your staff have sent for the {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} funding policy study. We now have the most recent valuation report, the participant data behind it, the plan document, and the trust statements. David has loaded the participant data, and the counts of active employees and retirees agree with the summary in the valuation report.

The count of former employees with deferred benefits does not agree: our file holds more of these records than the report shows. This is preliminary. One possible reason is that some of these people have already been paid, but we do not want to assume that, so I will post the list of records to our secure file transfer site this week and keep personal information out of email.

To keep the work moving, we would be grateful for the following:
1. Benefit statements, or a payment status from your records, for the former employees on that list.
2. A record of each contribution to the plan over recent plan years, with the amount and the deposit date.
3. The plan's current investment policy statement.
Robert would also like the working session we are arranging with you to cover the company's objectives for the policy. We will not model any alternative until those are agreed.

Sincerely,
Michelle
Funding Policy Study: Working Session Notes

We met with Lisa Hubbard to go over the baseline and to settle what {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} wants its funding policy to do. These notes are for the engagement file and for the company. Robert Lawrence prepared them.
Present
What we covered

1. The data. Michelle Banks reported that the checks on active employees and retirees are complete. The benefit statements Lisa Hubbard's staff sent us resolved most of the difference in the count of former employees with deferred benefits. The records that remain appear to belong to people who have already been paid. Lisa Hubbard will confirm this with the plan's recordkeeper. Until she does, we are keeping those records in the data and logging that as an assumption.

2. The baseline. David Sherman showed that our model reproduces the liabilities and the minimum required contribution in the most recent valuation report. The differences that remain are small, and he has traced each one to a known cause. We are satisfied the model is a sound place to start. It reflects the plan as of its last valuation date, and every projection we show will say so.
3. The company's objectives. We spent most of the session here. Lisa Hubbard told us what the company needs from the policy, and we wrote it down in her terms. She named four aims.

items: A contribution the company can set in its budget a year ahead.
Smaller swings in that contribution when interest rates move.
PBGC premiums counted as part of the cost of each policy.
A funded level that stays clear of the points at which the law restricts certain benefit payments.

blocks.text: We will send her a written summary of these aims to confirm. The recommendation will be judged against them, so we want the wording to be hers.

4. The alternatives. We agreed to model three policies beside the current practice. The first contributes the legal minimum each year. The second sets a level contribution for several years at a time and resets it on a schedule. The third aims to bring the plan to full funding over a fixed period. David Sherman will run them under a central set of assumptions first.

Lisa Hubbard asked whether a fourth policy, one that contributes enough each year to avoid the PBGC variable-rate premium, was worth modeling. It may turn out to sit close to the third. We agreed that David Sherman will show how near the third policy comes before we add another.

5. Scenarios. We also agreed to test each policy under lower investment returns and under a fall in interest rates. Robert Lawrence reminded the group that these are illustrations and not predictions. The report will keep the projected results apart from the assumptions behind them, and our judgment apart from both.
Actions agreed

rows: Confirm with the plan's recordkeeper whether the remaining former-employee records have been paid.
Send a written summary of the company's four aims for confirmation.
Run the current practice and the three alternatives under the central assumptions.
Show how near the third policy comes to removing the variable-rate premium.
Draft the two scenarios and circulate them internally before they are run.
Update the data log for the deferred-benefit records and the assumption held in their place.

blocks.text: Our next session will go through the projection results. We thank Lisa Hubbard and her staff for the work they have put into the data.
Funding Policy Study for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}}: Status at the Midpoint

Prepared by Michelle Banks, with David Sherman and Robert Lawrence. This report covers the period since our working session. It sets out where the study stands, what remains, and what could affect the schedule.
Where the study stands
The study is on schedule and within its fee. The data are settled, the baseline model is in place, and the company's objectives for the policy have been confirmed in writing.

David Sherman has run the current practice and the three alternative policies under the central assumptions. Those results are preliminary. Robert Lawrence has not yet reviewed them, and we have not formed a recommendation.
Nothing in this report is a finding. Where a statement depends on work still under review, it says so.

rows: Confirmed by the company in writing
Central runs done and awaiting review; scenario runs not started

blocks.text: Done since the working session

1. Data. Your staff confirmed through the plan's recordkeeper that the remaining former-employee records belong to people already paid. We have removed them from the projection data and recorded the change, with its source, in our data log.
2. Objectives. Robert Lawrence sent the written summary of the company's four aims, and the company confirmed it as written. Our recommendation will be measured against that summary.

3. Central projections. David Sherman projected contributions, funded status, and PBGC premiums for the current practice and each alternative. The starting point of every projection agrees with the most recent valuation report, as shown at the session. As agreed there, the results also show how near the third policy comes to removing the PBGC variable-rate premium.

4. Scenarios. The lower-return and falling-rate scenarios have been drafted and reviewed within our team. They will come to you with the preliminary results, so that you can see what each one assumes before anyone draws a conclusion from it.
Budget
The study is being performed for a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}. The work to date has stayed within the scope that fee covers, and we do not expect to ask for any change to it.
If the company asks for policies or scenarios beyond those agreed at the working session, we will describe the added work and its cost in writing before we begin it.
Next in the work
1. Robert Lawrence will review the central projections. Any correction he asks for will be made before results leave the firm.
2. David Sherman will run each policy under the two scenarios. We will report the results as a range across the scenarios, not as a single figure for each policy.
3. We will send you the preliminary results with a short note on how to read them. A second working session will follow to go through them with you.
4. Robert Lawrence will draft the report, with Michelle Banks writing the sections on data and methods. The draft will keep apart what the data show, what we assumed, and what we conclude.
5. Michelle Banks will check each policy's projected contribution against the legal minimum and the deduction limit in every projected year, so that no policy we present breaks either bound.
What could move the schedule

1. Interest rates. The projections begin from the assumptions of the most recent valuation. If rates have moved materially by the time we report, we will show the effect as a separate step and leave the baseline as it is.

2. Plan changes. The study assumes the plan's benefits stay as they are. If the company is considering a change to who may join the plan or how benefits are paid, we need to know before the scenario runs, because it would alter every projection.
3. The second working session. It needs the right people from the company in the room. Fixing a time for it early will help keep the draft report on schedule.
4. Preliminary figures. The central projections may change once Robert Lawrence has reviewed them. We ask that they not be circulated beyond the company's management until then.

5. Changes since the valuation date. The projections use the plan's membership as of its last valuation. A large change since then, such as a group of retirements, would be worth telling us about, even informally.
Questions about data can come to Michelle Banks, questions about the model to David Sherman, and questions of scope or judgment to Robert Lawrence.
